title: India-Born Republican Nirav Sheth Backs H-1B Crackdown, Citing Fake Firms
excerpt: Challenging Pramila Jayapal in Seattle, the former Marine says visa enforcement targets shell sponsors and falsified degrees — not legitimate Indian professionals.
body:
• Nirav Sheth, the India-born Republican challenging Rep. Pramila Jayapal in Washington's 7th District, has backed the Trump administration's H-1B crackdown, saying fake firms and falsified degrees are clogging the system.
  • Sheth, who moved to the US in 2008 and served in the Marine Corps, says the measures target shell sponsors, not technology giants or universities.
  • He declined to comment on the PERM suspension affecting Microsoft, Adobe and Infosys, citing an ongoing investigation, but acknowledged Indian professionals wait over a decade for green cards.
  • For Indian H-1B holders, the race matters because Indians accounted for around 70% of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2025, and the November 3 midterms will decide how far the crackdown goes.

Nirav Sheth, a Republican candidate for the US House of Representatives, has voiced strong support for the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration, arguing that the H-1B visa programme is being exploited by fraudulent firms at the expense of legitimate professionals, according to Times Now World.

Sheth was born in India and moved to the United States in 2008. He is running in Washington's 7th Congressional District against Democratic incumbent Pramila Jayapal, herself an Indian-American, in the November 3 midterm elections. A former member of the US Marine Corps and a former police officer, Sheth has made immigration enforcement a centrepiece of his campaign.

Fake firms are the target, Sheth says

Sheth contends that many companies sponsoring H-1B visas are essentially shell operations that lack genuine products or market solutions. Those firms, he argues, exploit legal loopholes and displace qualified individuals who have the documentation and education to contribute to the American economy.

He emphasised that the administration's restrictive policies are not aimed at established technology giants or academic institutions, but at eliminating the use of fake degrees and falsified documentation. By rooting out those practices, he said, the system can become more efficient for people who intend to work and live in the country legally. He advocates a case-by-case approach, with stricter enforcement alongside a restructured system that stays accessible to genuine contributors.

Silence on PERM, candour on the backlog

Asked about the administration's recent suspension of the PERM programme — the employment-based green card route linked to major corporations including Microsoft, Adobe and Infosys — Sheth remained cautious. Because an investigation is ongoing, he said he would not comment on the specific allegations against those companies.

He did, however, acknowledge the significant backlog facing Indian H-1B holders seeking green cards, noting that some professionals wait over a decade for permanent residency. That backlog is the lived reality for much of his own community: reporting on the midterms by IANS notes that at least nine Indian-American Republicans are on the November 3 ballot even as party leaders turn against the H-1B programme, and Vice President JD Vance has argued that most H-1B holders are used to replace American workers.

"Unfortunately, what we see with most H-1Bs is that you're taking somebody, I'm sure in most cases, a decent human being, and they're using them to replace an American middle class worker."

— JD Vance, US Vice President

What this means for Indian professionals

Sheth's stance puts him inside a tension now running through the Republican Party: the administration has imposed a $100,000 fee on certain H-1B petitions — since blocked by a second federal judge — and suspended the employment green card route for eight technology firms, while Indian-American candidates must also appeal to communities for whom those same visas are the main path to a life in the US.

Washington's 7th District, which covers most of Seattle, is strongly Democratic, and IANS rates Sheth's challenge as a long shot. But his argument — that fraud enforcement protects, rather than threatens, legitimate Indian applicants — is likely to be repeated by other candidates in the final week before November 3, and the outcome will shape whether the current restrictions harden into law or remain contested executive actions.
